analysis.one_liner: Requires companies to get consent before collecting or sharing a phone's location data.
analysis.headline: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved the bill in December 2012 and placed it on the Senate calendar, but the Senate never voted on it before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal violation for companies to knowingly collect, record, or share the location of a phone, car tracker, or other device without clear, separate consent from the person using it — not consent buried in a terms-of-use page. It would add criminal penalties for companies that knowingly help a stalker or domestic abuser track a victim, give federal and state enforcers and individuals the right to sue, and fund training for police and courts on location-based stalking. The bill cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee but never received a Senate floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who carries a phone or connected device. The bill's centerpiece is a consent rule: companies could not gather your location, or pass it to other companies, unless you affirmatively agreed after a clear notice showing what data is collected, who gets it, and how to withdraw. It specifically targets abusers who use location tracking to stalk partners, adds a crime for entities that knowingly aid interstate domestic violence or stalking by disclosing location data, bans selling location data on 1,000 or more children under 11, and funds law-enforcement training and a national study on location abuse in violence against women.

how_it_helps.text: Requires clear, separate on-screen consent before a company collects or shares device location data, displayed apart from end-user agreements or privacy policies, and lets individuals electronically revoke consent
Creates a crime, punishable by up to two years in prison, for a company or its employee that knowingly discloses a person's location to someone it knows could use it for domestic violence or stalking
Allows the U.S. Attorney General, state attorneys general, and aggrieved individuals to sue violators, with minimum damages of $2,500 per violation

Directs the Internet Crime Complaint Center to register complaints about location abuse in stalking, domestic violence, dating violence, and sexual assault, and authorizes grants to train police, prosecutors, judges, and victim-service personnel

analysis.who_pays: Companies that profit from location data — mobile app developers, mapping and location-based services, advertising networks, and data brokers — would bear new compliance costs, lose undisclosed collection and resale of location data, and face civil suits with statutory minimum damages of $2,500 per violation. Carriers and cable companies are largely carved out for ordinary network operation, which stays under existing Communications Act privacy rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: App makers, data brokers, ad networks

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall hardest on small app developers, who must build consent screens, disclosure notices, and revocation systems, and risk lawsuits with a $2,500 minimum damages award per violation

The bill allows one-time consent to cover ongoing collection, and a company that obtains location data from the company that first collected it needs no consent of its own — weakening the consent requirement as data moves through ad networks

Broad exceptions — for law enforcement and intelligence requests, protecting the company's own rights and property, fraud prevention, and network operation — leave large channels of location collection outside the consent rule
It preempts state laws that permit what the bill bans, though states may keep stronger protections

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: consumers gain control over who tracks them, and abusers lose an easy tool, while the app and advertising economy absorbs compliance costs and loses a revenue stream built on default location collection. The bill was softened in committee — one-time consent, an exemption for downstream companies, and a large law-enforcement exception — so it would not stop all location collection, but it would end the practice of collecting it silently.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved it with an amendment in December 2012 and put it on the Senate's waiting list for floor business, but the session ended three weeks later without the Senate ever voting on it.

narrative.text: Senator Franken introduced the bill on June 16, 2011 with six cosponsors — five Democrats and Independent Senator Sanders — and it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee

On December 13, 2012, the Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, and on December 17, 2012, Chairman Leahy reported it and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 567)
No floor vote ever occurred; the Senate adjourned on January 3, 2013 with the bill still awaiting action, and all Senate work on the bill died with the 112th Congress

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that profit from quietly collecting and reselling phone location data kept the status quo, and stalking victims gained no federal protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Location-data businesses kept the status quo

for.name: Sen. Al Franken
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and shepherded it through the Judiciary Committee, which approved it with an amended substitute

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill out of committee with an amendment on December 17, 2012, placing it on the Senate calendar

for.name: Domestic violence and stalking victim advocates
for.what_they_did: Backed the bill's anti-cyberstalking provisions; the bill directs consultation with national victim advocacy organizations and authorizes grants to victim-service personnel

against.name: Technology, app, and telecommunications companies
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill's consent and liability requirements, which would have restricted the collection and resale of device location data

against.name: Senate floor leadership
against.role: Senate Majority Leader and floor schedulers
against.what_they_did: Never brought the committee-approved bill to the floor for a vote in the three weeks it sat on the legislative calendar before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: All seven original sponsors were Democrats or the Independent Bernie Sanders, and no Republican cosponsored the bill; the Democratic-led Judiciary Committee nonetheless reported it favorably in the session's final weeks.

industries.industry: Mobile app developers and location-based services
industries.note: The bill would require clear, revocable consent before collecting or sharing a user's location, ending a default practice of silent collection. Compliance burdens are heaviest for small developers facing lawsuit exposure with $2,500 minimum damages.

industries.industry: Data brokers and mobile advertising networks
industries.note: These businesses buy and resell location data to target ads and other uses; the bill makes undisclosed collection and disclosure a federal violation enforceable by regulators, states, and individuals. One loopholes soften this: downstream companies buying data need no consent of their own.

The bill exempts activities governed by the Communications Act's carrier privacy provisions, so carriers keep collecting location data for network operation, but they could still face the new crime for knowingly disclosing a customer's location to a stalker.
